title: Condominium disputes
intro: This guide explains what Ontario's Condominium Act, 1998 and the Condominium Authority of Ontario say about condo disputes: the Condominium Authority Tribunal, the duty to follow the Act and the condo's documents, compliance orders in the Superior Court of Justice, and common expenses and liens. The regulation that lists which disputes the Tribunal hears is not covered, because the site does not yet have a source for it.

sections.heading: What the Condominium Authority Tribunal is
paragraphs: In this part of the Act, “Tribunal” means “the Condominium Authority Tribunal established under subsection 1.32 (1).” The Condominium Authority of Ontario describes it as “Canada’s first fully online tribunal”. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.31; condoauthorityontario.ca, Condominium Authority Tribunal — Dispute Resolution)

The Authority says: “Regulation 179/17 defines the scope of disputes that can be resolved by the Tribunal.” The site does not yet have a copy of that regulation, so this guide does not list the types of disputes it covers. (condoauthorityontario.ca, Condominium Authority Tribunal — Dispute Resolution)

Subject to one exception, “the Tribunal has exclusive jurisdiction to exercise the powers conferred on it under this Act and to determine all questions of fact or law that arise in any proceeding before it.” The exception: it “shall not inquire into or make a decision concerning the constitutional validity of a provision of an Act or a regulation.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.42)

sections.heading: Who can apply to the Tribunal, and about what
paragraphs: A condo corporation “may apply to the Tribunal for the resolution of a prescribed dispute with one or more of its owners or one or more occupiers or mortgagees of a unit.” An owner or a mortgagee of a unit “may apply to the Tribunal for the resolution of a prescribed dispute with the corporation, another owner or an occupier or a mortgagee of a unit.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (1), (2))

If the regulations so provide, a purchaser may apply about a dispute with the corporation regarding compliance with subsection 55 (3), “but not any other dispute.” An application “shall be in the form approved by the Tribunal.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (3), (5))

Some disputes cannot go to the Tribunal. These include a dispute about “Part III, section 20, 26, 82.1, 82.2, 85 or 86, subsection 117 (1) or Part VII or VIII”, and “a dispute involving the determination of title to any real property.” Sections 85 and 86 deal with the condo lien described below. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (4))

sections.heading: Time limits for Tribunal applications
paragraphs: “Subject to any other provision of this Act, an application must be made within two years after the dispute to which the application relates arose.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (6))

If that deadline is missed, “the Tribunal may extend the deadline for a time of no more than one additional year if the Tribunal is satisfied that the delay in not applying was incurred in good faith and no substantial prejudice will result to any person affected by the delay.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.36 (7))

Parties can settle. A signed written settlement “is binding on the parties.” A party who believes another party has broken the settlement may apply to the Tribunal “within six months after the contravention to which the application relates”, or later if the Tribunal is satisfied the delay “was incurred in good faith and no substantial prejudice will result to any person affected by the delay.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.47 (1), (3))

sections.heading: How a Tribunal case runs, and what it can order
paragraphs: A Tribunal proceeding “may be held orally or in writing, in person, by telephone, video conference or electronic mail, or through use of other electronic means in accordance with the rules of the Tribunal.” The Tribunal may direct the parties to take part in an “alternative dispute resolution mechanism”, which “includes mediation, conciliation, negotiation or any other means of facilitating the resolution of issues in dispute.” (Condominium Act, 1998, ss. 1.39 (2), 1.40)

The Tribunal may refuse to allow a person to make an application, or may dismiss an application without holding a hearing, if it “is of the opinion that the subject matter of the application is frivolous or vexatious or that the application has not been initiated in good faith or discloses no reasonable cause of action.” It may also dismiss without a hearing if the applicant filed documents “that the applicant knew or ought to have known to have contained false or misleading information.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.41)

Orders the Tribunal may make include an order “prohibiting a party to the proceeding from taking a particular action or requiring a party to the proceeding to take a particular action”, and an order to pay “compensation for damages incurred by another party to the proceeding as a result of an act of non-compliance up to the greater of $25,000 or the amount, if any, that is prescribed.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.44 (1))

The Tribunal may also order a party to pay the costs of another party or the costs of the Tribunal. Those costs are determined “in accordance with the rules of the Tribunal.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.44 (1), (2))

The Tribunal “shall not make an order requiring a person to vacate a property permanently.” The party against whom an order for compensation, costs or a penalty is made pays the amount “within 30 days, unless the order specifies another time limit.” (Condominium Act, 1998, ss. 1.44 (4), 1.45 (1))

A Tribunal order “is final and binding”, except that a party “may appeal the order to the Divisional Court on a question of law in accordance with the rules of court.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 1.46 (1), (2))

sections.heading: The duty to follow the Act, declaration, by-laws and rules
paragraphs: A condo corporation's objects “are to manage the property and the assets, if any, of the corporation on behalf of the owners.” It “has a duty to take all reasonable steps to ensure that the owners, the occupiers of units, the lessees of the common elements and the agents and employees of the corporation comply with this Act, the declaration, the by-laws and the rules.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 17 (1), (3))

The corporation, its directors, officers and employees, the declarant, an owner, an occupier of a unit and others listed “shall comply with this Act, the declaration, the by-laws and the rules.” An owner “shall take all reasonable steps to ensure that an occupier of the owner's unit and all invitees, agents and employees of the owner or occupier comply”. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 119 (1), (2))

A corporation, an owner and every person with a registered mortgage against a unit “have the right to require that a person who is required to comply with this Act, the declaration, the by-laws and the rules shall do so.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 119 (3))

sections.heading: Compliance orders in the Superior Court of Justice
paragraphs: An owner, a corporation, a mortgagee of a unit and others listed “may make an application to the Superior Court of Justice for an order enforcing compliance with any provision of this Act, the declaration, the by-laws, the rules” or certain agreements between corporations. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (1))

This court route does not apply “to any matter in dispute for which a person may apply for resolution under section 1.36 to the Condominium Authority Tribunal established under Part I.2, if the Tribunal has been established under that Part.” Also, if the mediation and arbitration processes in section 132 are required, a person may not apply “until the person has failed to obtain compliance through using those processes.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (2), (2.4))

On an application, the court may “grant the order applied for”, require payment of “the damages incurred by the applicant as a result of the acts of non-compliance” and “the costs incurred by the applicant in obtaining the order”, or “grant such other relief as is fair and equitable in the circumstances.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (3))

There is one limit on those orders. The court may not grant an order terminating a lease of a unit for residential purposes unless it is satisfied that the lessee has contravened an order made under subsection (3), or has received a notice described in subsection 87 (1) and “has not paid the amount required by that subsection.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (4))

If a corporation obtains an award of damages or costs against an owner or occupier of a unit, those amounts, “together with any additional actual costs to the corporation in obtaining the order, shall be added to the common expenses for the unit”, and the corporation may specify a time for payment by the owner. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 134 (5))

sections.heading: Common expenses and condo liens
paragraphs: “Subject to the other provisions of this Act, the owners shall contribute to the common expenses in the proportions specified in the declaration.” An owner is not exempt even if the owner “has waived or abandoned the right to use the common elements or part of them”, “the owner is making a claim against the corporation”, or the declaration, by-laws or rules restrict the owner's use. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 84 (1), (3))

If an owner defaults, “the corporation has a lien against the owner's unit and its appurtenant common interest for the unpaid amount together with all interest owing and all reasonable legal costs and reasonable expenses incurred by the corporation in connection with the collection or attempted collection of the unpaid amount.” (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 85 (1))

“The lien expires three months after the default that gave rise to the lien occurred unless the corporation within that time registers a certificate of lien in a form prescribed by the Minister.” “At least 10 days before the day a certificate of lien is registered, the corporation shall give written notice of the lien to the owner”. (Condominium Act, 1998, s. 85 (2), (4))

“The lien may be enforced in the same manner as a mortgage.” Upon payment of the amounts the certificate covers, the corporation “shall prepare and register a discharge of the certificate of lien” and advise the owner in writing of the particulars of the registration. A dispute about section 85 or 86 cannot be brought to the Tribunal. (Condominium Act, 1998, ss. 85 (6), (7), 1.36 (4))
